claim: Wikipedia (parts), Edinburgh council, French government sites, the University of Geneva, online shops and the BBC affected or taken offline
Found using frontier AI (ChatGPT) by Calif, then Wiz and OpenAI; 'a complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve'
Attackers could take control of affected web servers without authentication and steal data
by: Paul Spain, Gorilla Cyber Security; Woodward

claim: Calif 'mistakenly published a video' showing basic details of how the flaws could be used
by: PHP Foundation (as reported by the BBC)
note: Calif's own account needed

claim: The 'most severe' flaws ever detected by AI
No evidence yet that hackers have exploited the flaw
Where immediate remediation is not feasible, take the system offline until fully mitigated
by: UK NCSC; NSA; EU and Australian counterparts

claim: Amazon and Cloudflare saw sites being probed for the flaw
note: second-hand; need AWS or Cloudflare statements

claim: Something like 30 million websites could be affected
by: Alan Woodward, Surrey Centre for Cyber Security

claim: Roughly 70% of the internet is affected
note: BBC: 'unable to independently verify that figure'

claim: Two critical vulnerabilities
note: need the NSA post itself and the CVE IDs

claim: Criminals are using AI to 'vibe code' an attack method
Parts of Wikipedia, Edinburgh council, French government sites, the University of Geneva, online shops and the BBC were affected or taken offline
note: Not captured from any of the named organisations.

claim: Frontier AI found the flaw ahead of attackers, giving defenders time to prepare
note: Amazon reports an exploit attempt against a honeypot on 17 October, four days before disclosure, from an actor whose source of exploit information is unknown.

claim: The flaws were found by researchers using frontier AI under OpenAI's Patch the Planet initiative
note: All three research parties say AI was used. Calif: 'No special harness, or access to models that weren't generally available to everyone were used'. Calif does not name a model; Wiz names Gemini 4 Argon, GPT-5.6 Sol and Wiz Atlas; OpenAI's blog reportedly names GPT-5.6 Sol but is blocked.

claim: An exploit attempt hit an Amazon honeypot on 17 October from an anonymisation network, and proof-of-concept attempts started about 02:00 UTC on 21 October
by: CJ Moses, Amazon, via The Hacker News
note: Amazon's own post has not been found.

claim: Chainguard unilaterally broke the embargo on 21 October at 07:41 UTC by publishing built images containing the fix
note: Chainguard reportedly does not dispute the time but denies leaking (Techzine, blocked by a bot challenge; snippet only).

claim: CISA has not observed exploitation; neither CVE is in the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog
note: Catalog version 2026.10.21 fetched 2026-10-22T08:15Z, 1,754 entries. A point-in-time negative finding.

claim: Cloudflare observed attack traffic targeting its customers after the leak, with attackers mutating payloads
note: Primary party, no volumes.

claim: The flaws are CVSS 10.0
by: social posts on 20 October, relayed by a vendor and a news site
note: contradicted by a primary source. The PHP Foundation: 'a wrong CVSS score of 10.0 (the actual score is 9.2)'. Daubois traces it to a social post relayed by Phoenix Security and to watchTowr via Cyber Daily.

claim: The flaws were disclosed on 22 October 2026
note: contradicted by a primary source. Primary sources put the release at 21 October: GHSAs 13:34Z, tags 13:35Z, CVE records 13:48Z and 13:54Z, GitHub release 14:06Z.

claim: The fix removes longjmp() for out-of-memory errors in favour of a delayed soft OOM at the next VM safe point and a hard OOM via _exit(); the changelog line is 'Avoid state corruption via bailout'
The 8.5.12 fix may be incomplete, or there is a third, different bug
by: Fediverse posts relayed to oss-security by Aaron Rainbolt and Yves-Alexis Perez
note: Per a Matrix channel, Canonical asked PHP and 'was told that it's unrelated and not a real issue'. Second-hand. Nothing from PHP on the list at capture.

claim: The GitHub advisories credit four reporters: lcfr-hax (Calif), sagitzadik-wiz (Wiz), amyb-oai (OpenAI) and tomash-areion
note: tomash-areion is not named in the PHP Foundation's thanks and appears nowhere else on this beat.

claim: The risks require immediate patching across United States Government departments and agencies
note: No CISA emergency directive was visible on the CISA home page at capture.

claim: Automated exploitation attempts were seen in Latvia; none succeeded
note: Primary source.

claim: Latvia restricted access from abroad to several state digital resources, possibly until 26 October; lsm.lv and 112.lv were restored by 20:00 UTC
note: The one documented case of government services being pulled from the public internet, from the agency itself.

claim: On 20 October at about 15:00 UTC the two CVE IDs began circulating on forums and social media with a wrong release time and a wrong CVSS score; no technical details leaked
note: Primary party. The Foundation does not say who or where.

claim: The leak started with an anonymous Hacker News post citing a reliable source, which came down after screenshots spread; a screenshot of the 'PHP2Shell tool' credited to Calif.io and a short exploitation video also went up and came down
by: Alexandre Daubois (PHP security team, personal blog)
note: Contradicts the Foundation's 'no technical details leaked' and The Hacker News's 'a proof-of-concept exploit leaked'. No copy of the post, screenshot or video is in the vault.

claim: Mitigation advice given to a few critical-infrastructure providers from about 23:00 UTC on 20 October may have leaked

Calif mistakenly published a video around 20:00 UTC on 20 October showing its proof of concept against a number of targets; copies circulated and 'contributed to accelerated development of various PoCs'
note: Calif's own page does not mention a leak or a deleted video; it embeds two demo videos. Whether one of them is the deleted video is unknown.

claim: watchTowr confirmed in public that the bugs were real and posted both CVE numbers before the release
by: Daubois; CERT-EU lists a watchTowr X post among public reports

claim: The most severe flaws ever detected by AI
note: Wiz's own wording is 'among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history'. OpenAI: 'one of the most impactful vulnerabilities in recent memory'.

claim: There is no evidence yet that hackers have exploited the flaw
by: Ryan Austin, Calif, on Radio 4, 08:00 BST 22 October

claim: Reports of active exploitation exist
note: The only agency saying so, and it does not say whose reports.

claim: The UK's NCSC, the NSA and their counterparts in the EU and Australia advise taking systems offline where patching is not feasible
note: contradicted by a primary source. Australia's ACSC gives no offline advice. CERT-EU says isolate. The Netherlands, Italy, Japan and New Zealand give no offline advice.

claim: Organisations that cannot update immediately, or that run PHP 8.1 or older, should take PHP-based systems offline
'Where immediate remediation is not feasible, organisations should consider taking the system offline until it can be fully mitigated'
by: UK NCSC, as quoted by the BBC
note: That sentence is not on the NCSC page as captured at 08:09Z on 22 October. The page's offline advice is step 4 of 6 and is worded differently. The page was modified at 07:30Z that morning. The sentence's opening matches the Canadian CCCS text.

claim: If an immediate update is not feasible, take the system offline until it can be fully mitigated
note: X post 13:45:58Z 21 October (10.1 million views at capture) and the press release.

claim: Updating is the only complete mitigation; the configuration measures reduce exposure to specific paths and do not make an installation safe
OpenAI independently reported the same root cause on 11 August, with further vectors on 18 September
note: The GitHub advisories credit amyb-oai among four reporters. OpenAI's own post credits Calif's discovery 'using GPT-5.6 Sol' and Wiz; an X Community Note disputes OpenAI's role.

claim: The pre-announcement was published at 19:30 UTC on 20 October
note: The php.net feed says 20:32 UTC; oss-security relayed it at 20:22:51 UTC, so it was public by then.

claim: Amazon and Cloudflare saw sites being probed for the flaw
note: Second-hand, but consistent with what both companies have said themselves.

claim: The out-of-memory issue was found in a 2024 audit by Quarkslab (funded through OSTIF and the Sovereign Tech Agency) but exploitation was not proven, so it was not fixed
note: Two parties agree. The Foundation calls the delay 'a structural failure'. Cloudflare lists Quarkslab among the 2026 disclosers; nobody else does.

claim: Remote code execution is confirmed on PHP-FPM
by: PHP Foundation blog; GHSA-6wmf for the session path
note: GHSA-w8hw (CVE-2026-109618): 'no complete FPM exploit has been demonstrated for this SAPI'. The Foundation blog: RCE 'was also confirmed on PHP-FPM through application-level code paths'. GHSA-6wmf (CVE-2026-109619): session lifecycle RCE 'validated against mod_php and FPM'. The accounts may refer to different CVEs.

claim: Unauthenticated RCE over HTTP against Apache mod_php with default settings, before any application code runs
The release moved forward from 22 October 14:00 UTC to 21 October 14:00 UTC because of the leak
by: PHP Foundation; php.net pre-announcement; Wiz thread ('Apply the Oct 22 security release')
note: The php.net ChangeLog still dates all four releases 22 October. Wiz's X thread still says 22 October.

claim: The fixes were released at 14:00 UTC on 21 October
note: CERT-EU says 13:30 UTC; the tags and advisories are stamped 13:34 to 13:35 UTC; the GitHub release 14:06 UTC; the php.net feed entries carry 00:05 to 00:35 UTC, which are authoring times, not publication times.

claim: PHP is exposed on 2,608,039 internet-facing hosts
Something like 30 million websites could be affected
note: No basis given.

claim: Roughly 70% of the Internet is affected
by: Wiz (headline, X post); BBC attributing Wiz
note: The BBC was 'unable to independently verify that figure'. Wiz's body text says 70% of websites and cites no measurement.

claim: PHP is used by almost 70% of websites
by: Cloudflare; OpenAI ('an estimated 70%'); Wiz body text
note: None of the three cites the survey it comes from. A share of websites using PHP is an upper bound on exposure, not a count of vulnerable systems.

claim: About 6,000 potentially affected resources in Latvia, a few hundred in the public sector
note: Primary source, one country, says 'potentially'.

claim: 674 products in the NCSC-NL inventory: 206 vulnerable, 46 fixed, 418 under investigation, 3 not vulnerable
by: NCSC-NL, counted by this site from the file at commit cca173c64ec5
note: Counted, not quoted. NCSC-NL calls unbacked entries 'investigation leads'.

claim: Two critical vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, each CVSS v4.0 9.2, fixed in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35
All PHP versions from 5 onwards are affected by at least one of the flaws
note: The CVE records list only 8.2 to 8.5 with defaultStatus 'unaffected'. php.net published source backports for 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1, which implies they are affected. A scanner that trusts the CVE record will miss 7.4 to 8.1.

claim: Criminals are using AI to 'vibe code' an attack method
A web application firewall may provide some protection until systems are patched
note: Swiss BACS: 'Even a web application firewall alone is not sufficient.' Cloudflare says its rules blocked the traffic it saw and that attackers mutated payloads to get past them.

claim: Calif found the flaws first: discovery 1 August, hash commitment 5 August, report to PHP 11 August
note: The hash tweet is dated 5 August 2026 on X; its pre-image has not been published, so what it commits to cannot be checked.

claim: Wiz Research independently discovered the first flaw on 19 August and reported on 24 August
note: Wiz's X post says 'Wiz Research uncovers' with no credit to Calif or OpenAI; the blog thanks both.

claim: Pre-authentication RCE was confirmed against WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, MediaWiki, Roundcube, Magento, phpMyAdmin, Nextcloud, Laravel, Symfony and WHMCS
by: Calif; Wiz for WordPress and Drupal
note: Two researcher parties, no third-party reproduction in the vault. The demo videos were not downloaded.
